claim: Rodents have surpassed dogs and cats as the predominant model organisms to study pain since the 1980s.
source: Since the 1980s, rodents have surpassed dogs and cats as the predominant model organisms to study pain because of increased genetic access to their nervous system, ease of activating the pain system, and ability to work in a high-throughput manner testing many animals at once (Mogil, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mogil, 2009, which provides scholarly support for the historical shift in model organism preference.

claim: CGRP monoclonal antibodies work to block pain in rodents and effectively treat migraine pain in the clinic.
source: While translational impact has lagged behind basic science discoveries, there are still triumphs to note, such as CGRP monoclonal antibodies that work to block pain in rodents and effectively treat migraine pain in the clinic (Israel et al., 2018; Iannone et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Israel et al., 2018 and Iannone et al., 2022, which provide evidence for the efficacy of CGRP antibodies in both rodent models and clinical settings.

claim: Von Frey hair filaments have been used for more than 50 years to deliver mechanical stimuli to the mouse paw.
source: For more than 50 years, these stimuli have primarily been the von Frey hair (vFH) filaments that are delivered to the mouse paw from an experimenter below the rodent aiming, poking, and subsequently recording a paw lift (Frey, 1896; Dixon, 1980; Chaplan et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical work (Frey, 1896; Dixon, 1980; Chaplan et al., 1994) documenting the use of von Frey filaments.

claim: The experimenter has a greater effect on mechanical sensitivity test results than the mouse genotype.
source: A meta-analysis of thermal and mechanical sensitivity testing Chesler et al., 2002; Zumbusch et al., 2024 found that the experimenter has a greater effect on results than the mouse genotype, making data from different individual experimenters difficult to merge.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analyses (Chesler et al., 2002; Zumbusch et al., 2024) that quantified experimenter effects.

claim: Experimenter sex has a significant effect on mechanical sensitivity that appears to be mediated via stress.
source: Additional work has found that experimenter sex has a significant effect on mechanical sensitivity that appears to be mediated via stress (Sorge et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sorge et al., 2014, which provides evidence for sex-dependent experimenter effects.

claim: The ARM decreased the off-target distance of stimuli by 93.3% compared to manual delivery.
source: It was found that the ARM decreased the off-target distance of stimuli by 93.3% (Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing manual and ARM-based stimulus delivery accuracy, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ARM delivers more consistent stimulus based on analysis of stimulus height with high-speed videography.
source: It was found that the ARM decreased the off-target distance of stimuli by 93.3% (Figure 1C), while delivering more consistent stimulus based on analysis of stimulus height with high-speed videography (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Videos 3–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from high-speed video analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Videos 3–6.

claim: No significant differences were found in open field test measures when the ARM was running versus silent.
source: No significant differences were found in distance traveled, center entrances, center, time in center, and latency to center entrance based on a Student's two-tailed t-test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of open field test data comparing ARM noise conditions, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: The ARM does not induce an increased stress state due to its noise, even in non-habituated mice.
source: Based on this, neither stress nor locomotion differences were detected by this test, indicating the ARM does not induce an increased stress state due to its noise, even in non-habituated mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of significant differences in open field test measures, which are used to assess stress and locomotion.

claim: Researcher 1 delivered max average forces of 1.5 g and 2.7 g with 1.4 g and 2 g von Frey filaments.
source: With the same 1.4 g and 2 g von Frey filaments, Researcher 1 delivered max average forces of 1.5 g and 2.7 g, and Researcher 2, 1.35 g and 2.4 g.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of force application using a force sensor.

claim: The ARM delivered average max forces of 1.36 g and 1.9 g with 1.4 g and 2 g von Frey filaments.
source: The ARM delivered average max forces closest to the targeted forces, with 1.36 g and 1.9 g (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2B and C comparing ARM force application to target forces.

claim: The ARM had no variation in stimulus delivery time, whereas manual stimulus delivery had an average 12.4% variation.
source: The ARM had no variation in stimulus delivery time, whereas manual stimulus delivery had an average 12.4% variation in the stimulus length of individual researchers and 61.17% variation in that of the combined researchers (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by coefficient of variation calculations from experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The ARM decreased the time needed to apply a stimulus 10 times to a mouse paw by 50.9% compared to manual delivery.
source: Further, we found that the ARM decreased the time needed to apply a stimulus 10 times to a mouse paw by 50.9% compared to manual delivery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental timing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Researcher 2 elicited a significantly higher paw withdrawal frequency than Researcher 1.
source: However, a two-way ANOVA and a post hoc Tukey test found that Researcher 2 elicited a significantly higher (p=0.0008) paw withdrawal frequency than Researcher 1 (Figure 2G)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental behavioral data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No significant differences were found between researchers applying ARM stimulus remotely.
source: Comparisons between the third and fourth researchers applying ARM stimulus remotely found no significant differences in response to either individual vFH or the full dataset (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Pinprick stimuli elicited significantly decreased withdrawal latency compared to cotton swab stimuli.
source: Testing of C57BL/6J (n=15) at baseline found significant decreases in withdrawal latency for pinprick compared to cotton swab stimuli delivered in identical ways by the ARM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) based on a two-tailed Student's t-test.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental withdrawal latency data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mice injected with carrageenan showed elevated shaking behavior in response to pinprick stimuli compared to baseline.
source: Mice injected with carrageenan (n=15) showed elevated shaking behavior (p=0.038, two-way ANOVA, post hoc Tukey test) in response to pinprick stimuli in comparison to measurements at baseline (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from a carrageenan pain model shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The force ramp stimulus successfully detected carrageenan hypersensitivity to touch.
source: The force ramp stimulus successfully detected carrageenan hypersensitivity to touch (Figure 3G), with a significant decrease in mechanical threshold from baseline for the ipsilateral paw but not the contralateral control (p=0.027, two-way ANOVA post hoc Tukey test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of mechanical threshold data from a carrageenan pain model shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Catch trials found a 96% response rate in true trials, with only a 7% rate in catch trials.
source: These trials found a 96% response rate in true trials, with only a 7% rate in catch trials, indicating responses were not being driven by device noise (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from catch trial analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Remote-habituated mice showed a significant decrease in time to rest over 3 days compared to mice habituated with a researcher present.
source: Remote habituated mice showed a significant decrease (p=0.0217, two-way ANOVA) in time to rest over the 3 days (Figure 4B), but no significant differences for any single day.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of habituation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Remote-habituated mice showed significantly less turning on day 2 compared to mice habituated with a researcher present.
source: It was found that remote-habituated mice showed significantly less turning on day 2 compared to mice habituated with a researcher present (p=0.024, two-way ANOVA post hoc Tukey test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of turning behavior during habituation.

claim: Only the remote-habituated mice showed significantly decreased turning behavior on day 3 compared to day 1.
source: and that only the remote-habituated mice showed significantly decreased turning behavior on day 3 compared to day 1 (p=0.0234, two-way ANOVA post hoc Tukey test) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of turning behavior data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mice take longer to habituate to experimental conditions when an experimenter is present.
source: These findings indicate that mice take longer to habituate to experimental conditions when an experimenter is present – a result consistent with mice being prey animals on heightened alert for danger.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the habituation data and interpreted in the context of mouse behavior as prey animals.

claim: Cotton swab stimuli elicited increased male mouse reflexive paw withdrawal features when Researcher 1 was present compared to when no researcher was present.
source: A two-way ANOVA and a post hoc Tukey test found that cotton swab stimuli elicited increased male mouse reflexive paw withdrawal features, including max paw height (p=0.0413) and max paw velocity (y-axis) (p=0.042) when Researcher 1 was present compared to when no researcher was present (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Pinprick stimuli led to increased max paw height and max paw velocity in male mice compared to female mice when Researcher 1 was present.
source: Pinprick stimuli (Figure 4H and I), on the other hand, led to increased max paw height (p=0.044) and max paw velocity (y-axis) (p=0.041) in male mice compared to female mice when Researcher 1 was present.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: Male mice showed significantly increased paw distance traveled compared to female mice when Researcher 2 was present in response to cotton swab.
source: For cotton swab (Figure 4G), male mice showed significantly increased paw distance traveled compared to female mice when Researcher 2 was present (p=0.047, two-way ANOVA post hoc Tukey test) but not when Researcher 2 was present or no researcher was present.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Female mice showed significantly decreased mechanical threshold compared to male mice when a male researcher was present.
source: It was found that female mice showed significantly decreased mechanical threshold compared to male mice (p=0.034, Šídák's multiple comparisons test and Student's t-test) when a male researcher was present.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of mechanical threshold data from experiments with different researcher genders.

claim: Sex-dependent differences in evoked pain behavior can appear and disappear based on which researcher is in the room.
source: These findings indicate that sex-dependent differences in evoked pain behavior can appear and disappear based on which researcher/s are in the room.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results showing variable sex differences depending on experimenter presence.

claim: Reflexive features including paw withdrawal latency and max paw height showed significant correlations with stimulus intensity in male mice.
source: Analysis of the resulting withdrawal responses in male mice using PAWS and linear regression found both features with significant positive linear relationships with stimulus intensity and features where no significant correlation could be found. Reflexive features including paw withdrawal latency (Figure 5B) and max paw height (Figure 5C) showed significant correlations with stimulus intensity that explained 26.9% and 13.8% of the variation in the data, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Affective features including paw shaking duration and paw distance traveled showed either no significant correlation or weak correlation with stimulus intensity.
source: In contrast, analysis of affective features, including paw shaking duration (Figure 5D) and paw distance traveled (Figure 5E), found either no significant correlation or a correlation that only explained 6.596% of the variation in the data.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Stimulus variability has a greater effect on the mouse's initial reflexive response than the following affective features.
source: This data indicates that in isolation, stimulus variability has a greater effect on the mouse's initial reflexive response than the following affective features.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of correlation strengths between reflexive and affective features with stimulus intensity.

claim: Each of the three stimulus types led to significant up/downregulation of BLA neural activity compared to background.
source: Each of the three stimulus types led to significant up/downregulation of neural activity compared to background (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by peri-event analysis of neural activity data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: 29.3% of neurons were regulated by mechanical pain, 10.7% by touch, and 11.4% by both mechanical stimuli.
source: Neurons were registered across consecutive days to identify neurons regulated by mechanical pain (29.3%), touch (10.7%), or both (11.4%) mechanical stimuli (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell registration analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Cotton swab events showed a significantly smaller proportion of pain matching downregulation, upregulation, or combined group regulation compared to the pinprick stimuli.
source: Cotton swab events showed a significantly smaller proportion of pain matching downregulation, upregulation, or combined group regulation compared to the pinprick stimuli (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neural regulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Downregulated and total mechanical pain neuron proportions correlate with withdrawal latency.
source: Our results on withdrawal latency were consistent with previous work (Corder et al., 2019) that found that BLA mechanical pain neural activity correlates with this metric, with downregulated (p=0.0032) and total mechanical pain neuron (p=0.0047) proportions correlating with withdrawal latency based on a Pearson correlation, total cell proportion explaining 8.54% of the variation in the data (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis of neural activity and behavioral data shown in Figure 6I, and is consistent with prior work (Corder et al., 2019).

claim: Paw distance traveled and max y-velocity each show correlations with up, down, and total regulated mechanical pain cells.
source: In comparison, paw distance traveled (Figure 6J) and max y-velocity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) each show correlations with up (p=0.0014, p=0.0324), down (p=0.0062, p=0.0009), and total (p=0.0003, p=0.0007) regulated mechanical pain cells, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis of neural activity and behavioral data shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Max y-velocity and paw distance traveled may be more useful metrics for the study of the BLA's role in pain compared to max paw height or withdrawal latency.
source: These findings suggest that max y-velocity and paw distance traveled may be more useful metrics for the study of the BLA's role in pain compared to max paw height or the traditionally used withdrawal latency.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of correlation strengths between different behavioral metrics and BLA neural activity.

claim: The ARM is an effective tool for efficiently correlating in vivo imaging data with evoked behavioral data, including sub-second behavior.
source: This data indicates that the ARM is an effective tool for efficiently correlating in vivo imaging data with evoked behavioral data, including sub-second behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the successful integration of ARM stimulus delivery with microendoscopy and behavioral analysis.

claim: The brain is important for pain from sensory perception to encoding affective components of pain that negatively alter mood and motivation.
source: With this said, the brain is also important for pain – from sensory perception to encoding affective components of pain that negatively alter mood and motivation (Cai et al., 2018; Corder et al., 2019; Chiang et al., 2020; Starr et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the brain's role in pain processing.

claim: The basolateral amygdala has been linked to encoding pain affect, unpleasantness, and negative emotion.
source: Finally, we combine ARM stimulation with in vivo brain recording in the basolateral amygdala, an area that has been linked to encoding pain affect, unpleasantness, and negative emotion (Corder et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2022; Becker et al., 2023; Tanimoto et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the BLA's role in pain affect.

claim: Electronic von Frey and dynamic plantar aesthesiometer still require an experimenter to be present and are focused on measuring a mechanical force threshold.
source: Previous attempts to decrease this variability in mechanosensory testing have focused on eliminating variability in stimulus delivery with devices such as electronic von Frey and the dynamic plantar asthesiometer, but both still require an experimenter to be present and are focused on measuring a mechanical force threshold, limiting their ability to measure hyperalgesia (Möller et al., 1998; Raposo et al., 2015; Urru et al., 2020; Jokinen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on these devices and their limitations.

claim: The ARM was built using a series of linear stages, cameras, and stimulus holders.
source: Built using a series of linear stages, cameras, and stimulus holders, the ARM is more accurate at hitting the desired target, delivers stimuli faster, and decreases variability in delivery of von Frey hair filaments.
evidence: This claim describes the physical construction of the ARM device.

claim: The ARM enables remote testing of mice with experimenters outside the testing room.
source: Importantly, the ARM enables remote testing of mice with experimenters outside the testing room.
evidence: This claim describes a key capability of the ARM device demonstrated in the study.

claim: Experimenter presence led to significant sex-dependent differences in paw withdrawal and pain-associated behaviors.
source: Using remote testing, we found that mice habituated more quickly when an experimenter was not present, and experimenter presence led to significant sex-dependent differences in paw withdrawal and pain-associated behaviors.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from remote testing experiments comparing conditions with and without experimenter presence.

claim: The ARM can be combined with cellular-resolved microendoscopy in the amygdala to link stimulus, behavior, and brain activity.
source: Lastly, to demonstrate the utility of the ARM for neural circuit dissection of pain mechanisms, we combined the ARM with cellular-resolved microendoscopy in the amygdala, linking stimulus, behavior, and brain activity of amygdala neurons that encode negative pain states.
evidence: This claim describes the integration of ARM with brain imaging technology demonstrated in the study.

claim: Three linear stages were mounted and wired together to allow for controlled and customizable movement of the stimulus along the x-, y-, and z-axis.
source: To this end, three linear stages were mounted and wired together to allow for controlled and customizable movement of the stimulus along the x-, y-, and z-axis.
evidence: This claim describes the technical design of the ARM device.

claim: A final rotational axis was attached to the z-axis to allow for both the controlled application of a brush stimulus and the quick switching of stimuli.
source: A final rotational axis was attached to the z-axis to allow for both the controlled application of a brush stimulus and the quick switching of stimuli.
evidence: This claim describes a technical feature of the ARM device design.

claim: The device was redesigned so that it could fit on a 75 cm×50 cm table.
source: This device was then redesigned so that it could fit on 75 cm×50 cm table, using three 500 frames per second (fps) cameras and a force sensor to aid in stimulus delivery (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim describes a design modification to the ARM device.

claim: The ARM was controlled with a custom-built Python code that paired the standard Xbox One controller to the bottom-up camera.
source: We controlled the ARM with a custom-built Python code that paired the standard Xbox One controller to the bottom-up camera, with calibrated crosshairs superimposed on the camera's video feed.
evidence: This claim describes the control system for the ARM device.

claim: Remote desktop software was used to allow for control of the device from either across the lab or even across the city.
source: Remote desktop software was then used to allow for control of the device from either across the lab or even across the city (Video 1).
evidence: This claim describes the remote control capability of the ARM, demonstrated in Video 1.

claim: Noise generated by the ARM was observed to be minimal compared to the background HVAC noise.
source: Noise generated by the ARM was observed to be minimal compared to the background HVAC noise.
evidence: This claim is based on observational comparison of noise levels.

claim: PAWS features measured from 500 fps video data were not significantly different from the 2000 fps data based on a two-way ANOVA.
source: PAWS features measured from 500 fps video data were not significantly different from the 2000 fps data based on a two-way ANOVA.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing behavioral features extracted from different frame rate videos.

claim: The 500 fps camera paired with PAWS was found to be sufficient to distinguish between cotton swab and pinprick withdrawal responses.
source: The camera paired with PAWS was found to be sufficient to distinguish between cotton swab and pinprick withdrawal responses, suggesting it may be a useful tool for labs that cannot invest in a more expensive device.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation of the lower-cost camera system.

claim: The PAWS software was updated to allow for simple installation on new devices and a full graphical interface.
source: To facilitate high-throughput analysis, the PAWS software was updated to allow for simple installation on new devices and a full graphical interface.
evidence: This claim describes software improvements made to the PAWS analysis tool.

claim: Features were added to PAWS to allow for the analysis of SLEAP tracking data, greater control over feature scoring, and support for ARM-assisted measurement of withdrawal latency.
source: In addition, features were added to allow for the analysis of SLEAP tracking data, greater control over feature scoring, and support for ARM-assisted measurement of withdrawal latency.
evidence: This claim describes new features added to the PAWS software.

claim: Von Frey filaments never bend back to the exact same position.
source: During the previously described von Frey experiments, it was observed that vFHs never bend back to the exact same position.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from von Frey experiments.

claim: A new force sensor-guided stimulus was developed to provide a more accurate method for measuring withdrawal latency and improving stimulus accuracy.
source: To address this, a more accurate method for measuring withdrawal latency and improving stimulus accuracy, a new force sensor-guided stimulus was developed.
evidence: This claim describes a technical innovation in the ARM device.

claim: The force sensor stimulus can apply a force ramp where the force exerted on the mouse paw will increase from 0.5 to 8 g over the course of 5 s.
source: The two primary ways it is used are to either apply a force ramp where the force exerted on the mouse paw will increase from 0.5 to 8 g over the course of 5 s (Figure 3D)
evidence: This claim describes a specific stimulus delivery mode of the force sensor, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The force sensor stimulus can apply a consistent force where stimulus velocity will be adjusted up and down to maintain a consistent force on the paw.
source: or a consistent force where stim velocity will be adjusted up and down to maintain a consistent force on the paw (Figure 3E) for a force and duration of the researcher's choice.
evidence: This claim describes another stimulus delivery mode of the force sensor, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Upon paw withdrawal, the force sensor stimulus retracts automatically and max force is reached, and withdrawal latency is reported.
source: Upon paw withdrawal, the stimulus retracts automatically and max force is reached, and withdrawal latency is reported.
evidence: This claim describes the automated measurement capability of the force sensor stimulus.

claim: The force ramp stimulus found significant decreases comparing baseline to 24 hr for the ipsilateral paw and ipsilateral to contralateral at the 24 hr time point in the CFA model.
source: The force ramp again found significant decreases were found both comparing the baseline to 24 hr for the ipsilateral paw (p=0.026) and ipsilateral to contralateral at the 24 hr time point (p=0.044) (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of CFA pain model data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The 1 g stimulus found a highly significant decrease in withdrawal latency for the ipsilateral paw in the CFA model.
source: Finally, the 1 g stim found a highly significant decrease in withdrawal latency for the ipsilateral paw (p<0.0001) (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of CFA pain model data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Mice responded 6.6% of the time to catch trials and 95.8% to trials that made contact with the paw.
source: Catch trials performed during carrageenan experiments found mice responded 6.6% of the time to catch trials and 95.8% to trials that made contact with the paw, a significant decrease (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from catch trial analysis.

claim: Mechanical withdrawal latency can reliably distinguish between responses to noxious and innocuous mechanical stimuli in rodents.
source: This decrease was found in both male and female mice, indicating that mechanical withdrawal latency can reliably distinguish between responses to noxious and innoxious mechanical stimuli in rodents.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistent finding of decreased withdrawal latency to pinprick vs cotton swab across sexes.

claim: Variability in stimulus intensity in isolation contributes significantly to the resulting paw withdrawal response.
source: In summary, variability in stimulus intensity in isolation contributes significantly to the resulting paw withdrawal response, though it appears to primarily affect the initial reflexive response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation analysis between stimulus intensity and behavioral features.

claim: Withdrawal percentage, withdrawal latency, and withdrawal threshold are the most commonly used measures of mechanical sensitivity/pain and are based on the reflexive behavioral response.
source: It should be noted that withdrawal percentage, withdrawal latency, and withdrawal threshold are the most commonly used measures of mechanical sensitivity/pain and are based on the reflexive behavioral response that is significantly correlated with stimulus variability.
evidence: This claim draws on established knowledge about common pain measurement methods and connects it to the study's findings.

claim: The basolateral amygdala was chosen based on previous work that has identified neural populations linked to defensive coping behaviors like paw attending, paw guarding, and paw shaking.
source: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) was chosen based on previous work that has identified neural populations linked to defensive coping behaviors like paw attending, paw guarding, and paw shaking (Corder et al., 2019; Jones et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work identifying BLA's role in pain-related behaviors.

claim: Previous work has identified both excitatory neural populations in the BLA that when activated lead to increased or decreased pain behavior.
source: This has included both the identification of excitatory neural populations that when activated lead to increased (Becker et al., 2023; Han et al., 2010) or decreased (Cai et al., 2018) pain behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on BLA neural populations and pain modulation.

claim: The ARM democratizes the study of pain by removing the need to have a well-trained researcher spending hours aiming at the rodent paw.
source: The ARM democratizes the study of pain by removing the need to have a well-trained researcher spending hours aiming at the rodent paw.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the broader impact of the ARM technology.

claim: Researchers outside the pain field studying autism, neurodegeneration, or social isolation have reported somatosensory deficits.
source: Moreover, researchers outside the field – such as those studying autism, neurodegeneration, or social isolation, all of which have reported somatosensory deficits (Orefice et al., 2016; O'Leary et al., 2018; Crane et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2023; Horiguchi et al., 2013) – might have an easier time phenotyping their animals with the ARM.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work documenting somatosensory deficits in various conditions.

claim: Traditional somatosensory assays are physically taxing and are not options for some researchers with physical disabilities.
source: It can also not be ignored that traditional somatosensory assays are physically taxing and are not the options for some researchers with physical disabilities – challenges the ARM overcomes in many ways.
evidence: This claim draws on general knowledge about the physical demands of manual stimulus delivery and infers accessibility benefits of the ARM.

claim: A company named Tactorum Inc has been formed to promote the widespread adoption of the ARM device.
source: To promote the widespread adoption of this device across as many labs as possible, a company named Tactorum Inc has been formed.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the commercialization of the ARM technology.

claim: All experimental testing was performed in compliance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (NIH), with approved IACUC protocol number AC-AABL6560.
source: All experimental testing was performed in compliance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (NIH), with approved IACUC protocol number AC-AABL6560.
evidence: This is a factual statement about ethical compliance of the research.

claim: C57BL/6J mice were ordered from Jackson Laboratories.
source: C57BL/6J mice were ordered from Jackson Laboratories.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the source of experimental animals.

claim: Male and female mice ranging from 8 to 16 weeks in age were used for testing.
source: Over the course of the experiments, male and female mice ranging from 8 to 16 weeks in age were used for testing.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Mice were allowed to acclimate to their housing for 2 weeks before testing.
source: Mice were allowed to acclimate to their housing for 2 weeks before testing.
evidence: This is a factual statement about experimental procedures.

claim: Before somatosensory testing, mice were habituated for 4 days, 1 hr each, to testing conditions.
source: Before somatosensory testing, mice were habituated for 4 days, 1 hr each, to testing conditions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about experimental procedures.

claim: For experiments where only remote ARM work would be performed, only 1 day of habituation was found to be needed.
source: For experiments where only remote ARM work would be performed, only 1 day of habituation was found to be needed.
evidence: This claim is based on empirical observation during experimental optimization.

claim: The ARM is the intellectual property of Columbia University.
source: The ARM is the intellectual property of Columbia University, so we are limited in the extent to which we can share building instructions or other such details.
evidence: This is a factual statement about intellectual property ownership.

claim: The current version of the ARM device is licensed by and made available by Tactorum Inc.
source: That said, the current version of the device is licensed by and made available by Tactorum Inc.
evidence: This is a factual statement about device licensing and availability.

claim: The PAWS pipeline is freely available for installation and use on GitHub.
source: Our PAWS pipeline is freely available for installation and use on GitHub (https://github.com/osimon81/PAWS, copy archived at Ogundare, 2023).
evidence: This is a factual statement about software availability.

claim: Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were injected with AAV9-syn-jGCaMP8f-WPRE virus and implanted with integrated lenses via stereotaxic surgery.
source: Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were injected with AAV9-syn-jGCaMP8f-WPRE virus (Addgene #162376-AAV9) (jGCaMP8f) and implanted with integrated 0.6 mm × 7.3 mm lens with attached baseplates (Inscopix cat. #1050-004413) via stereotaxic surgery in a single-step procedure.
evidence: This is a factual statement about surgical procedures for brain imaging experiments.

claim: Viruses were injected and lenses implanted at coordinates AP: –1.6 mm, ML: 3.2 mm, DV: –4.5 mm to target the BLA.
source: Viruses were injected and lenses implanted at the following coordinates to target the BLA: (AP: –1.6 mm, ML: 3.2 mm, DV: –4.5 mm).
evidence: This is a factual statement about stereotaxic coordinates used for targeting the BLA.

claim: The virus was allowed to express for 4 weeks before imaging.
source: Mice were treated with meloxicam for 3 days post-surgery, and the virus was allowed to express for 4 weeks before imaging.
evidence: This is a factual statement about experimental timeline for viral expression.

claim: Calcium imaging data was collected using the Inscopix nVista system at frame rate 20–25 Hz and LED power 0.5 mW/mm2.
source: Calcium imaging data was collected using the Inscopix nVista system (Inscopix Data Acquisition Software [IDAS Version 1.3.0]). Recordings were taken under the conditions: frame rate = 20–25 Hz, LED power = 0.5 mW/mm2, and a gain and focus that optimized image resolution and GCaMP expression for each mouse.
evidence: This is a factual statement about imaging parameters.

claim: Videos were automatically spatially downsampled by 4 by the data acquisition software, as recommended by the manufacturer.
source: Videos were automatically spatially downsampled by 4 by the data acquisition software, as recommended by the manufacturer.
